concepts.title: The phases of an ambulance call
key_points: A call has phases that begin before the tones and end after you are back in quarters
Preparation is the phase most often skipped and the one that decides the others
Dispatch gives you the location, the nature, and often information you should act on before arrival
En route is the time to plan: roles, equipment, hazards and what you expect to find
Arrival begins with scene size-up, not with patient contact
Patient care, then packaging, then transport, with the destination decision made deliberately
Transfer of care means a verbal handover to someone of equal or higher training, and it is not complete until they accept it
Post-run is a real phase: cleaning, disinfection, restocking, refuelling and completing the report
The unit is not available again until it is genuinely ready, and saying so is part of the job
Every phase has a failure mode, and most in-service failures trace back to preparation or post-run
misconceptions: Treating the call as beginning at the tones
Skipping size-up and walking straight to the patient
Leaving a patient without a verbal handover
Marking available before the unit is restocked
exam_favorites: Transfer of care is a handover

read.plain:
It helps to think of a call as having phases, because each one has its own job and its own characteristic failure.

Preparation comes first, and it happens long before the tones. The vehicle checked, the equipment present and working, the oxygen full, the batteries charged, you fed and rested and knowing where things are. This is the phase people skip, and it is the phase that decides how all the others go. Everything you discover at three in the morning that is missing was missing at the start of the shift as well.

Dispatch gives you a location, a nature, and often more than people use. Listen properly. There is frequently information in there that should change something before you arrive — the number of patients, a hazard, a weapon mentioned, a location you know.

En route is planning time, and it is underused. Who is taking the patient and who is driving? What are you bringing in? What do you expect to find and what would change that? Is there a hazard? Two minutes of this on the way makes the first two minutes on scene dramatically better.

Arrival begins with size-up, not with patient contact. Scene safe, hazards, number of patients, mechanism, additional resources. Walking straight to the patient is how crews get hurt and how second patients get missed.

Then patient care, then packaging, then transport, with the destination chosen deliberately — by patient need, protocol and capability, not by habit.

Transfer of care is a phase in its own right and it is a frequent failure point. It means giving a verbal handover to someone of equal or higher training, and it is not complete until they have accepted the patient. Leaving someone on a bed in a corridor and putting a form in a tray is not transfer of care; in many systems it is abandonment. Say it out loud, say the important thing first, and make sure the person you told is the person taking over.

Post-run is a real phase with real work in it: cleaning, disinfection, restocking, refuelling, completing the report, and getting the crew ready for the next one. This phase gets rushed because the call feels over, and that is exactly how the next crew ends up short of something.

And the rule that ties it together: the unit is not available until it is genuinely ready. There is real pressure to mark available quickly, and resisting that when you are not actually ready is part of the job rather than a failure to do it.
read.standard: EMS responses comprise sequential phases, each with distinct objectives and characteristic failure modes. Preparation precedes dispatch and comprises vehicle inspection, equipment verification and function testing, consumable stocking, and provider readiness; deficiencies identified during a call originate in this phase. Dispatch provides location, nature and frequently additional actionable information including patient numbers, hazards and weapon involvement, warranting attentive receipt. The en route phase permits role assignment, equipment selection, hazard anticipation and formulation of expectations. Arrival commences with scene size-up addressing safety, hazards, patient count, mechanism and resource requirements, preceding patient contact; omission is associated with provider injury and missed additional patients. Subsequent phases comprise patient assessment and care, packaging, and transport with destination selected by patient need, protocol and facility capability. Transfer of care requires verbal handover to a provider of equal or higher training and is incomplete until acceptance; documentation alone without verbal transfer may constitute abandonment. The post-run phase comprises decontamination, disinfection, restocking, refuelling, report completion and crew readiness, and is subject to compression owing to perceived completion. Unit availability should be declared only upon genuine readiness notwithstanding operational pressure.

eli_new.analogy: Everything you find missing at three in the morning was missing at the start of the shift too. Preparation is the phase that decides every other one.
eli_new.body: Transfer of care is not finished when you put the form in the tray. It is finished when a person of equal or higher training has heard your handover and accepted the patient.

teach.prompt: Walk through the phases of an ambulance call and name each phase's failure mode.

Dispatch often carries information that should change something
En route is planning time: roles, equipment, hazards
Arrival begins with size-up, not patient contact
Destination is chosen by need, protocol and capability

A form in a tray is not transfer of care
Post-run is a phase and the unit is not available until ready

story.title: Available
story.dispatch: Medic 4 — clearing the hospital, dispatcher asking for status.
story.body:
There was pressure on and they were being asked to go available before the vehicle had been touched.

The officer said they would be available in six minutes, and listed what still needed doing.

Six minutes later they took a call that needed two of the things on that list.

concepts.title: Daily readiness and vehicle checks
key_points: Check the vehicle and the equipment at the start of every shift, without exception
A check is not a glance — things are tested, not merely observed to be present
Test what has to work: suction, oxygen flow, batteries, lights, the stretcher's locks
Check quantities and check expiry dates, because both fail silently
Check the vehicle itself: fuel, fluids, tyres, lights, brakes and the warning devices
Use the checklist your service provides rather than your memory, which will skip the same item every time
Fix or report anything found, and document it — an unreported fault is a fault nobody fixes
Know where everything is, because in the dark you will find things by memory rather than by looking
The previous crew may have been busy, so assume nothing about what was restocked
The oxygen cylinder is the classic failure: full at the start of the shift is not full now
misconceptions: Looking at equipment rather than testing it
Trusting that the previous crew restocked
Skipping expiry dates
Finding a fault and not reporting it

read.plain:
Check the vehicle and the equipment at the start of every shift. Every shift, not most shifts, and not only when you have time — because the shift where you skip it is statistically going to be the one where it matters.

And understand what a check actually is. A check is not a glance along a shelf confirming that objects exist. Things get tested. Turn the suction on and listen to it pull. Open the oxygen and watch the flow. Switch the monitor on and confirm the battery is charged. Work the stretcher and hear the locks engage. Equipment that is present and broken is worse than equipment that is missing, because you will discover it at the moment you were relying on it.

Check quantities and check dates. Both fail quietly. A box with two left in it looks the same as a full one from a distance, and an expired item looks exactly like a current one. Those are the two things a quick look will never catch, which is precisely why they are on the list.

Check the vehicle as a vehicle, not just as a box of equipment. Fuel, fluids, tyres, lights, brakes, wipers, and the warning lights and siren. The clinical kit is useless in a vehicle that will not get you there.

Use the checklist your service provides. Not because your memory is bad, but because memory skips reliably — people miss the same item every time and never notice, and a written list is the only thing that catches it.

Anything you find, fix it or report it, and document that you did. A fault that is noticed and not reported is a fault nobody fixes, and it will be found again by the next crew under worse conditions.

There is a second purpose to the check that people miss. Doing it teaches you where everything is. On a bad call in the dark you will reach for things rather than search for them, and that only works if your hands already know the layout. Crews who check properly are faster on scene, and that is not a coincidence.

Assume nothing about the previous crew. They may have had a difficult night and run out of time. That is not a criticism of them; it is the reason the check exists.

And know the classic failure, which is oxygen. A cylinder that was full at the start of your last shift is not full now, and a cylinder someone used and put back looks identical to a full one. Read the gauge. Every time.
read.standard: Vehicle and equipment inspection is performed at the commencement of every shift without exception. Inspection comprises functional testing rather than visual confirmation of presence: suction generation, oxygen flow, battery charge state, warning device operation and stretcher locking mechanisms are tested in operation, as present but non-functional equipment presents greater hazard than absent equipment. Quantity and expiry verification are required, as both fail without visible indication. Vehicle inspection addresses fuel, fluid levels, tyres, lighting, braking, wipers and emergency warning devices. The service-provided checklist should be used in preference to recall, as memory omission is systematic and unrecognised. Identified deficiencies require rectification or reporting with documentation; unreported faults persist to subsequent crews under less favourable conditions. Inspection additionally establishes equipment location familiarity, supporting retrieval by proprioception rather than search under adverse operational conditions. No assumption should be made regarding restocking by the preceding crew. Oxygen cylinder pressure constitutes a characteristic failure point, as partially depleted cylinders are visually indistinguishable from full cylinders and gauge verification is required at each inspection.

eli_new.analogy: Equipment that is present and broken is worse than equipment that is missing, because you find out at the exact moment you were counting on it.
eli_new.body: A check tests things. Turn the suction on and listen to it. A glance along a shelf tells you objects exist, which is not the question you needed answered.

The cylinder looked exactly the same as a full one, because they all do.

Somebody read the gauge anyway, out of habit, and it read half.

The call ninety minutes later ran the whole way in on oxygen.

concepts.title: Safe emergency driving
key_points: Lights and sirens ask other drivers for permission to proceed — they do not create right of way
Due regard means you remain responsible for driving safely regardless of your warning devices
Most people do not react to sirens the way you expect: they stop suddenly, turn in, or do not hear you at all
Modern cars are extremely well insulated, so your siren reaches far less far than you assume
Intersections are where ambulances crash — slow down, cover the brake, and make eye contact before proceeding
Clear each lane separately at an intersection rather than treating it as one decision
Speed saves very little time on most responses and costs enormously when it goes wrong
Everyone must be restrained, including the crew in the back wherever it is possible
Unsecured equipment becomes a projectile in a collision, so stow everything
A crash converts one emergency into several and removes the resource that was coming to help
misconceptions: Believing warning devices grant right of way
Assuming drivers can hear the siren
Treating an intersection as a single decision
Leaving equipment unsecured in the patient compartment

read.plain:
Start with the thing that is most often misunderstood. Lights and sirens do not create right of way. They request it. They ask other drivers for permission to proceed, and permission can be refused, ignored, or simply not heard. In most jurisdictions your warning devices allow you to ask for certain exemptions, and they never relieve you of the duty to drive safely. That duty is usually called due regard, and it is the legal standard you will be measured against if anything goes wrong.

So think about what actually happens when other drivers meet you.

Some stop dead in the middle of the road, which is the commonest reaction and the one that catches people out. Some panic and turn into your path. Some pull to the left when they meant to pull to the right. Some do exactly the right thing. And a substantial number never hear you at all.

That last group is larger than people assume. Modern cars are extremely well insulated, with the windows up, climate control on, and music or a phone call playing. A siren that is deafening in your cab may be barely audible in theirs until you are close enough for it to be useless. Never assume you have been heard. Assume the opposite and drive accordingly.

Intersections are where ambulances crash. It is not the open road and it is not the speed on the straight; it is the junction. So build a habit there. Slow down meaningfully on approach. Cover the brake. Change the siren tone, because a changing sound is noticed where a constant one becomes background. And clear the intersection lane by lane rather than treating it as a single go or no-go decision — each lane is a separate vehicle that has to be seen to have stopped. Make eye contact where you can. A driver who has looked at you is a driver who has seen you; a driver looking at their phone has not, whatever their car is doing.

On speed: it saves very little. Over a typical response, driving considerably faster produces a difference measured in a small number of minutes, and almost never changes the outcome for the patient. The cost when it goes wrong is a collision involving your crew, your patient and members of the public. The arithmetic is not close.

Inside the vehicle: everyone restrained, including the crew in the back wherever the care being given allows it. And stow everything. Loose equipment in a collision becomes a projectile travelling at the speed the vehicle was travelling, and the patient compartment is full of heavy objects.

The summary that makes all of this stick: a crash turns one emergency into several, and it removes the resource that was on its way to help.
read.standard: Emergency warning devices request rather than confer right of way; permission may be refused, disregarded or unperceived. In most jurisdictions warning devices permit request of specified exemptions while preserving the duty to operate safely, a standard designated due regard, which constitutes the applicable legal measure. Anticipated motorist responses include abrupt stopping within the carriageway, movement into the path of the emergency vehicle, movement in the incorrect direction, appropriate yielding, and complete failure to perceive the warning. Contemporary vehicle sound insulation, closed windows, climate control and audio substantially attenuate siren audibility, and audibility should not be assumed. Intersections constitute the predominant site of ambulance collision; risk mitigation comprises meaningful deceleration on approach, brake covering, siren tone variation as constant tones are perceptually filtered, lane-by-lane clearance rather than single-decision assessment, and eye contact confirmation. Increased response speed yields minimal time saving over typical response distances with negligible outcome effect, against substantial collision consequence. Occupant restraint applies to all persons including rear compartment personnel where patient care permits. Equipment must be secured, as unsecured objects become projectiles at vehicle velocity within a compartment containing substantial masses. Collision converts a single emergency into multiple incidents and removes the responding resource.

eli_new.analogy: The siren is a request, not a command. Permission can be refused, and quite often it is never even heard.
eli_new.body: Clear an intersection lane by lane. It is not one decision about whether the junction is clear; it is a separate decision about each vehicle that has to have stopped.

story.title: She never heard it
story.dispatch: Medic 7 — responding, approaching a green light at speed.
story.body:
The light was green and technically nothing was required of them at all.

The driver slowed anyway and covered the brake, out of habit rather than for a reason.

The car that came through the red never braked, and the driver was still looking straight ahead as she passed.

concepts.title: Scene positioning and roadway safety
key_points: Roadway incidents are among the most dangerous things EMS does, and responders are struck and killed doing them
Park to protect the working area, not for your own convenience in leaving
Position upwind and uphill of any potential hazard, and beyond the scene where fuel or fluids may spread
Use the vehicle as a physical barrier between traffic and the people working
Leave warning lights on, but be aware that too many lights can confuse and attract drivers
Wear high-visibility clothing on every roadway incident, without exception
Never turn your back on traffic, and work facing oncoming vehicles where possible
Get the patient out of the traffic lane as soon as it is safe to do so
Load from the protected side, and keep everyone out of the lane while doing it
Approaching traffic includes drivers who are distracted, impaired or looking at the incident rather than the road
misconceptions: Parking for convenience of departure
Working with your back to traffic
Skipping high-visibility clothing for a quick job
Loading from the traffic side

read.plain:
Roadway incidents are among the most dangerous things EMS does. Responders are struck and killed on roads, doing ordinary work, on calls that were not otherwise remarkable. It is worth treating with the seriousness it deserves rather than the routine it feels like.

Start with parking, and the principle that governs it: park to protect the working area, not for your own convenience in leaving. The instinct is to position for a clean exit, and that instinct puts the vehicle in the wrong place.

What you want is the vehicle placed so that it shields the space where people will be working. Angle it so that if something strikes it, it is pushed away from the working area rather than into it. Your service will have a policy on this and it will be specific about angles and distances — learn it.

Position upwind and uphill of any potential hazard, so smoke, vapour or fumes blow away from you rather than over you, and so spilled fuel does not run towards where you are standing. And park beyond the scene rather than short of it where fluids may be spreading.

Leave warning lights on, with one caveat worth knowing: too many lights can confuse approaching drivers, and there is a well-documented phenomenon where drivers steer towards the thing they are looking at. Follow your service's guidance on which lights to leave running, because more is not automatically better.

Wear high-visibility clothing on every roadway incident. Every one, including the quick ones, including in daylight, including when you are only going to be there two minutes. The calls where people get hit are precisely the ones that felt too brief to bother.

Never turn your back on traffic. Work facing oncoming vehicles where you can, and if you must turn away, have someone else watching. This is a habit you build deliberately, because the natural thing is to focus entirely on the patient and forget that there is a road behind you.

Get the patient out of the traffic lane as soon as it is safe to do so. Every minute spent working in a live lane is exposure for everybody, and the assessment you could do at the roadside can almost always be done in the ambulance instead.

Load from the protected side, with everyone out of the lane while you do it. That moment — stretcher out, doors open, several people concentrating on lifting — is one of the most exposed of the whole call.

And hold on to the honest picture of approaching traffic. It contains drivers who are distracted, drivers who are impaired, drivers who are tired, and drivers who are looking directly at your incident instead of at the road. You are not being protected by anyone's attention. Assume the worst driver on that road is about to arrive, and set the scene up for them.
read.standard: Roadway incidents represent a leading hazard to EMS personnel, with responder fatalities from vehicle strikes occurring during routine operations. Vehicle positioning should prioritise protection of the working area over departure convenience, with angling such that impact displaces the vehicle away from rather than into the working space; service-specific policy defines angles and distances. Positioning should be upwind and uphill of potential hazards to direct smoke, vapour and spilled fluids away from personnel, and beyond rather than short of the incident where fluid spread is possible. Warning lights should remain operational subject to service guidance, as excessive illumination may confuse approaching drivers and target fixation directs vehicles toward illuminated objects. High-visibility apparel is required at all roadway incidents without exception, including brief daylight operations, as short-duration exposures are associated with strike events. Personnel should avoid turning away from traffic, working facing oncoming vehicles where practicable with designated observation otherwise. Patient extraction from live traffic lanes should occur as soon as safely achievable, with assessment relocated to the vehicle. Loading should occur from the protected side with all personnel clear of live lanes, this phase representing a period of maximal exposure. Approaching traffic should be presumed to include distracted, impaired, fatigued and incident-focused drivers, and scene configuration should assume the least attentive driver.

eli_new.analogy: Assume the worst driver on that road is about to arrive, and set the scene up for them. Nobody's attention is protecting you.
eli_new.body: Park to protect the working area, not to make leaving easy. The instinct to position for a clean exit puts the vehicle in exactly the wrong place.

concepts.title: Air medical transport
key_points: Air transport is requested for time-critical patients where it meaningfully shortens definitive care time
It is not automatically faster — count the launch, flight, landing, loading and flight time honestly
Weather, aircraft availability and darkness can all make air transport unavailable, so have a ground plan
Request early if you are going to request at all, because the aircraft takes time to arrive
The landing zone must be flat, firm, clear of wires, poles, trees, loose debris and people
Wires are the principal hazard and they are extremely hard to see from the air — report them specifically
Loose material becomes a projectile in rotor wash, so clear or secure everything nearby
Nobody approaches the aircraft until a crew member signals, and then only from the front, in the pilot's view
Never approach from the rear, because the tail rotor is effectively invisible when turning
On sloping ground approach from the downhill side, where the main rotor sits higher above the ground
misconceptions: Requesting air transport without counting the total time honestly
Failing to report wires at the landing zone
Approaching the aircraft before being signalled
Approaching from the rear or from the uphill side
exam_favorites: Approach from the front when signalled

read.plain:
Air medical transport exists for time-critical patients where flying meaningfully shortens the time to definitive care. That is the test, and it is worth applying honestly.

Because air transport is not automatically faster. Count the whole thing: the time for the aircraft to launch, the flight to you, the landing, the handover and loading, then the flight to hospital. On a short transport to a nearby capable facility, a ground ambulance that is already on scene with the patient in it will frequently win. Ask yourself whether the aircraft genuinely shortens time to definitive care, not whether it is more impressive.

Availability is real too. Weather stops aircraft flying, and it stops them at short notice. Aircraft are often already committed elsewhere. Darkness and terrain limit some operations. So always have a ground plan, and do not let a requested aircraft become the reason a patient is still on scene twenty minutes later.

And if you are going to request, request early. The aircraft cannot be somewhere it has not been asked to go, and cancelling later costs nothing compared with requesting late.

Then the landing zone, which is your job and is where you can do real harm or real good.

It needs to be flat, firm and clear. Flat enough to land on, firm enough not to sink or throw up dust and debris, and clear of obstructions in every direction — wires, poles, trees, signs, fences, vehicles and people.

Wires deserve their own paragraph because they are the principal hazard in this whole activity and they are extremely hard to see from the air. Overhead power lines, telephone lines, guy wires on poles, and anything strung between two points. If there are wires anywhere near your landing zone, say so explicitly and say where they are. Do not assume the crew can see what is obvious to you from the ground.

Loose material becomes a projectile. Rotor wash is far stronger than people expect and it will pick up loose debris, blankets, equipment, dust, hats, unsecured dressings and paperwork, and throw them at the aircraft and at everybody standing nearby. Clear or secure everything in the area before the aircraft arrives, including your own kit.

Now the approach rules, which are simple and absolute.

Nobody approaches the aircraft until a crew member signals them to. Nobody. The pilot and crew control that space, and approaching without a signal is how people get hurt.

When signalled, approach from the front, where the pilot can see you. Stay in their field of view the whole way. Never approach from the rear, because the tail rotor is turning at a speed that makes it effectively invisible and there is nothing to see until it is far too late.

And on sloping ground, approach from the downhill side. The main rotor tilts toward the uphill side, which brings the blades lower to the ground exactly where a person walking uphill would meet them.
read.standard: Air medical transport is indicated for time-critical patients where its use meaningfully reduces time to definitive care. The determination requires honest accounting of total elapsed time including aircraft launch, transit to scene, landing, patient transfer and loading, and transit to the receiving facility; ground transport frequently proves superior for short distances to capable facilities with the patient already loaded. Availability limitations include weather, which may preclude flight at short notice, prior commitment of aircraft, and darkness or terrain restrictions; a ground transport contingency should always exist and a requested aircraft should not prolong scene time. Requests should be initiated early, as cancellation carries minimal cost relative to delayed request. Landing zone requirements comprise level, firm ground clear of obstructions including wires, poles, trees, signage, fencing, vehicles and personnel. Overhead wires constitute the principal hazard and are poorly visible from the air; their presence and location require explicit communication. Rotor downwash generates projectiles from loose material, requiring clearance or securing of debris, equipment, linen and documentation prior to arrival. Approach is prohibited until signalled by a crew member. Approach occurs from the front within the pilot's field of view and is maintained throughout. Rear approach is prohibited owing to the effectively invisible rotating tail rotor. On sloping terrain approach occurs from the downhill aspect, as main rotor tilt reduces blade ground clearance on the uphill side.

eli_new.analogy: The tail rotor is turning fast enough to be invisible. There is nothing to see and nothing to hear in time, which is why the rule is absolute rather than a matter of care.
eli_new.body: Wires are the thing that kills aircraft and they are nearly impossible to see from above. If there are any near your landing zone, say so out loud and say exactly where.

story.title: Say where they are
story.dispatch: Engine 8 — landing zone being established in a field beside a road.
story.body:
The field was flat and firm and completely clear, and somebody said so on the radio.

Then they added that there was a single telephone line across the far corner, running to a farmhouse, and gave the direction.

The pilot said afterwards that they would not have seen it.

concepts.title: Body mechanics and safe lifting
key_points: Back injury ends more EMS careers than anything dramatic, and it accumulates rather than arriving
Lift with the legs, keep the back straight, and never twist while under load
Keep the weight as close to your body as possible — distance multiplies the load on your spine
Feet shoulder width apart, weight balanced, and a firm grip with the palms up where you can
Communicate before and during every lift so everyone moves at the same moment
One person calls the lift, and everyone else lifts on their count rather than their own judgement
Know your limits and ask for help before you start, not once you are committed
Use equipment that does the work for you wherever it is available — that is what it is for
Push rather than pull where you have the choice, and work at waist level where you can
The most dangerous moments are the unplanned ones: an awkward corner, a sudden shift, a stumble
misconceptions: Twisting while carrying a load
Holding the weight away from the body
Asking for help only after the lift has started
Lifting on your own count rather than the caller's

read.plain:
Back injury ends more EMS careers than anything that would make the news. And it rarely arrives as a single dramatic event. It accumulates — a slightly wrong lift, a twist under load, an awkward corner, hundreds of times, until one ordinary movement is the one that does it. Which means the habits you build now matter more than any single lift.

The mechanics are simple enough to state.

Lift with your legs, which are built for it, rather than with your back, which is not. Keep your back straight — straight, not necessarily vertical. Bend at the hips and knees.

Never twist while under load. This is the single most important rule in the whole topic. The spine tolerates compression reasonably well and tolerates rotation under load very badly. So if you need to change direction while carrying, move your feet and turn your whole body. The instinct to swivel at the waist because your feet are planted is exactly the movement that injures people.

Keep the weight close to your body. This one is underappreciated, and the physics is unforgiving: the further the load is from your spine, the greater the effective force on it, and the multiplication is dramatic rather than gradual. A weight held at arm's length loads your back several times more than the same weight held against your chest. So get close before you lift, and stay close while you carry.

Stance: feet about shoulder width apart, weight balanced between them, and a firm grip. Where you have the choice, grip with the palms up, which is stronger and more stable than palms down.

Then communication, which is the part crews actually get wrong most often. Talk before the lift: who is where, what is the plan, where are we going, what happens at the door. Talk during it. And have one person call the lift, with everybody moving on that person's count — not on their own assessment of when things look ready. Two people lifting a quarter of a second apart means one of them briefly took the whole weight, and that is a classic injury.

Know your limits, and ask for help before you begin. Once the lift is underway you are committed, and a request for help at that point is a request to rescue you. Asking at the start costs you a minute and nothing else.

Use the equipment. Stair chairs, powered stretchers, lifting sheets, slide boards — they exist precisely so that human backs do not have to do the work, and there is nothing impressive about doing it the hard way.

Push rather than pull where you have the choice, because pushing uses larger muscle groups and keeps the load closer. Work at waist level where you can, and avoid lifting from the floor when there is any alternative.

And know where the danger concentrates. It is not the straightforward lift you planned for. It is the unplanned moment: the corner that turned out to be tighter than it looked, the patient who shifted suddenly, the person who stumbled and whose share of the weight moved to everyone else without warning. Plan the route, walk it first if you need to, and slow down at the awkward parts.
read.standard: Musculoskeletal back injury constitutes the leading cause of career termination in EMS and typically results from cumulative rather than singular mechanism. Correct technique comprises lifting with the lower limbs rather than the lumbar spine, maintaining a straight back with flexion at hip and knee. Rotation under load is the principal prohibited movement, as the spine tolerates axial compression considerably better than loaded rotation; directional change while carrying requires repositioning of the feet and rotation of the whole body. Load proximity to the body is critical, as the moment arm increases spinal loading disproportionately with distance; loads held at arm's length impose several times the spinal loading of the same mass held against the trunk. Stance comprises feet at approximately shoulder width with balanced weight distribution and a secure grip, with supinated grip preferred where available. Communication requirements comprise pre-lift briefing addressing positions, plan, route and obstacles; continued communication during movement; and designation of a single individual to initiate the lift, with all personnel moving on that count rather than independent judgement, as asynchronous lifting transiently loads individual providers. Personal limits should be assessed and additional assistance requested before commencement rather than during an executed lift. Mechanical aids including stair chairs, powered stretchers, lifting sheets and slide boards should be used where available. Pushing is preferred to pulling, and work at waist height is preferred to floor-level lifting. Injury risk concentrates in unplanned events including constricted routes, sudden patient movement and provider stumbling.

eli_new.analogy: The spine handles being squashed reasonably well and handles being twisted under load very badly. Move your feet.
eli_new.body: Distance multiplies. The same weight held at arm's length loads your back several times more than held against your chest, so get close before you lift and stay close while you carry.

concepts.title: Emergency, urgent and non-urgent moves
key_points: How you move a patient depends on why you are moving them and how much time you have
An emergency move is used when the danger of staying outweighs the risk of moving
Three reasons for an emergency move: immediate danger, inability to reach another patient, or care that cannot be given where they are
Emergency moves accept a risk of worsening injury because the alternative is worse
Drag along the long axis of the body wherever possible to limit spinal movement
Common emergency moves include clothes drags, blanket drags, shoulder drags and the firefighter's carry
An urgent move is used when the patient's condition requires quicker movement than a routine transfer
The rapid extrication technique is an urgent move, used for condition rather than convenience
Non-urgent moves are planned and unhurried, and this is where most patient movement happens
Speed is never a reason on its own — the justification is danger or condition, not schedule
misconceptions: Using an emergency move for convenience or speed
Dragging across the body rather than along its long axis
Using rapid extrication because the scene is awkward
Treating non-urgent moves as unimportant
exam_favorites: Three reasons for an emergency move

read.plain:
How you move a patient depends on two things: why you are moving them, and how much time you have. Those give you three categories, and the distinction between them is a distinction of justification rather than technique.

An emergency move is used when the danger of staying where they are outweighs the risk of moving them badly. That is the whole test, and it is worth stating clearly because an emergency move genuinely does accept a risk of worsening an injury. You do it anyway, because the alternative is worse.

There are three accepted reasons.

First, immediate danger to the patient or the crew — fire, explosion risk, structural collapse, hazardous material, an unsafe scene, rising water, traffic.

Second, you cannot reach another patient who needs care without moving this one.

Third, the care the patient needs cannot be given where they are. The classic example is a patient in cardiac arrest in a seated position, or on a bed you cannot compress against. The intervention requires them somewhere else, so they go somewhere else.

When you do perform one, the technique principle is to drag along the long axis of the body wherever possible — pull from the shoulders or the clothing so the whole body moves in line, rather than dragging sideways which bends and twists the spine. The common versions are the clothes drag, the blanket drag, the shoulder or armpit drag, and, where one person must move someone quickly, a firefighter's carry. You are not trying to protect the spine perfectly; you are trying to protect it as much as an emergency allows.

An urgent move sits in the middle. The patient's condition requires them moved more quickly than a routine, unhurried transfer would allow, but there is no immediate environmental danger. The rapid extrication technique from a vehicle is the standard example: the patient's condition means they need to be out now, so they come out with manual spinal stabilisation and speed rather than with the full sequence.

And the discipline to hold on to here is that an urgent move is justified by condition, not convenience. Rapid extrication because the patient is deteriorating is correct. Rapid extrication because the vehicle is an awkward shape and the full method would take longer is not.

Non-urgent moves are the planned, unhurried ones, and they are the overwhelming majority of patient movement. There is no immediate threat and the patient's condition allows you to do it properly: choose the right device, position it well, get enough people, brief the lift, and move deliberately. The fact that these are routine does not make them safe — most of the back injuries happen here, simply because this is where most of the lifting is.

The summary: speed is never a justification on its own. The justification is danger or condition, and if neither applies, you have time to do it properly.
read.standard: Patient movement is categorised by justification and available time. Emergency moves are indicated where the hazard of remaining in position exceeds the risk of movement, and explicitly accept potential injury exacerbation. Three accepted indications exist: immediate danger to patient or providers including fire, explosion risk, structural instability, hazardous materials, scene insecurity, water ingress or traffic; obstruction of access to another patient requiring care; and inability to deliver required care in the present position, exemplified by cardiac arrest in a seated position or on a non-rigid surface. Technique prioritises traction along the longitudinal body axis, applied at the shoulders or clothing, to limit lateral spinal flexion and rotation; recognised methods comprise the clothing drag, blanket drag, shoulder or axillary drag, and single-provider carries. Urgent moves are indicated where patient condition requires expedited movement absent immediate environmental hazard, exemplified by rapid extrication from a vehicle with manual spinal stabilisation. Justification is patient condition rather than operational convenience; extrication difficulty or time saving do not constitute indications. Non-urgent moves comprise planned, unhurried transfers where neither hazard nor condition compels expedition, permitting device selection, positioning, adequate personnel and briefed execution, and constitute the majority of patient movement and consequently the majority of provider injury. Expedition alone does not justify categorical escalation.

eli_new.analogy: An emergency move accepts that you might make an injury worse. You do it because staying is worse still, and that trade is the whole definition.
eli_new.body: Rapid extrication because the patient is deteriorating is correct. Rapid extrication because the car is an awkward shape is not. Condition, never convenience.

concepts.title: Devices and when to use each
key_points: Choosing the right device is most of what makes a move safe and comfortable
The wheeled stretcher is the default for transport, and is loaded and unloaded to a procedure
A stair chair moves a seated patient down stairs, and needs a patient who can tolerate sitting up
A scoop stretcher splits lengthways and assembles under a patient with minimal movement
A long backboard is an extrication and movement device, not a comfortable transport surface
A vacuum mattress conforms to the patient and is more comfortable and more stable for long journeys
A basket stretcher is for rough ground and technical rescue where wheels are useless
A flexible stretcher moves a patient through narrow or awkward spaces
Slide sheets and transfer boards move a patient sideways between surfaces with much less effort
Every device has weight limits and a correct procedure — improvising with an unfamiliar device is how people get dropped
misconceptions: Using a stair chair for a patient who cannot tolerate sitting
Leaving a patient on a long board for a long transport
Improvising with an unfamiliar device
Ignoring a device's weight limit
exam_favorites: Board is not a transport surface

read.plain:
Most of what makes a move safe and comfortable is choosing the right device before you start. The lift technique matters, but the device decides how hard the lift has to be in the first place.

The wheeled stretcher is the default for transport. It carries the patient for the bulk of the journey and it loads and unloads to a specific procedure — learn yours, because loading is a moment with a known injury pattern, and powered models have their own sequence that must be followed rather than approximated.

A stair chair moves a seated patient down stairs, and it is enormously better than carrying someone on a stretcher down a staircase. The condition it imposes is that the patient must be able to tolerate sitting upright: not someone with a suspected spinal injury, not someone hypotensive who deteriorates when sat up, not someone who cannot maintain the position. Many models have tracks for descending stairs, which are far safer than lifting each step.

A scoop stretcher splits lengthways into two halves that assemble underneath a patient from either side. Its virtue is that you can get it under someone with very little movement of the patient, which makes it excellent where you want to lift someone off the ground without rolling them.

A long backboard is an extrication and movement device. It is worth saying plainly that it is not a comfortable or benign transport surface — prolonged time on a rigid board causes pain and pressure injury, and practice in most systems has moved away from transporting patients on one. Use it to move someone, then follow your protocol for what they travel on.

A vacuum mattress conforms to the patient's shape when the air is drawn out, becoming rigid while spreading the load. It is more comfortable and more stable than a rigid board, especially for longer journeys and rough ground, where a patient on a flat board slides and a patient in a vacuum mattress does not.

A basket stretcher is for rough ground and technical rescue — down a slope, across a field, off a trail, out of a confined space, on a rope system. Anywhere wheels are useless and the patient must be carried by hand.

A flexible stretcher wraps around the patient and is for narrow, awkward spaces: tight staircases, small bathrooms, corridors with sharp turns, where a rigid device simply will not go round the corner.

And slide sheets and transfer boards, which are the most underused equipment in the service. Moving a patient sideways between two surfaces at the same height is where a great deal of unnecessary lifting happens, and a slide sheet turns a lift into a slide. Use them.

Finally: every device has a weight limit and a correct procedure. Exceeding the limit is how equipment fails, and improvising with a device you have not used before is how patients get dropped. If you do not know a device, say so before the lift rather than during it.
read.standard: Device selection substantially determines the safety and comfort of patient movement and precedes technique in importance. The wheeled stretcher constitutes the default transport device, with model-specific loading and unloading procedures; loading carries a recognised injury pattern and powered models require adherence to their specific sequence. Stair chairs facilitate seated movement on stairways and are contraindicated where the patient cannot tolerate upright positioning, including suspected spinal injury, hypotension with positional intolerance, and inability to maintain posture; tracked models permit controlled descent. Scoop stretchers separate longitudinally and assemble beneath the patient bilaterally, permitting placement with minimal patient movement and avoidance of log-rolling. Long backboards constitute extrication and movement devices rather than transport surfaces; prolonged immobilisation produces pain and pressure injury, and contemporary practice in most systems avoids transport upon them. Vacuum mattresses conform to patient contour on evacuation of air, providing rigidity with load distribution, superior comfort and stability over extended transport and uneven terrain. Basket stretchers serve rough terrain and technical rescue where wheeled transport is impracticable. Flexible stretchers accommodate confined and angular spaces inaccessible to rigid devices. Slide sheets and transfer boards facilitate lateral transfer between surfaces of equivalent height, converting lifting to sliding, and are substantially underutilised. All devices carry weight limits and defined procedures; limit exceedance produces equipment failure and unfamiliar device improvisation produces patient drops.

eli_new.analogy: A slide sheet turns a lift into a slide. Moving somebody sideways between two beds is where an enormous amount of unnecessary lifting happens.
eli_new.body: The long board is a device for moving people, not a surface for lying on. Use it to get them somewhere, then follow your protocol for what they actually travel on.

concepts.title: Packaging, positioning and securing
key_points: Packaging means preparing the patient for movement so that nothing shifts and nothing is forgotten
Position by condition: the position that helps this patient is a clinical decision, not a default
Sit a patient with breathing difficulty up, unless their condition prevents it
Position a patient with reduced consciousness who is breathing to protect their airway
Shock positioning varies between systems — follow your protocol rather than a remembered rule
Secure the patient to the device, then secure the device to the vehicle — both, every time
Straps must be snug enough to hold in a sudden stop, and checked again after moving
Secure the legs as well as the chest, because a patient slides downwards on inclines and stairs
Protect against cold at every stage, since patients cool while being moved and cold worsens outcomes
Keep tubing, lines, monitors and oxygen where they will not be caught, pulled or trapped
misconceptions: Securing the patient but not the device
Leaving straps loose enough to allow sliding
Using a remembered shock position rather than the protocol
Forgetting the patient is getting cold during the move

read.plain:
Packaging means preparing the patient for movement so that nothing shifts, nothing is caught and nothing is forgotten. It is the step that gets rushed, and it is the step that decides whether the journey is safe.

Start with position, and treat it as a clinical decision rather than a default. The right position depends on the patient's condition.

A patient with breathing difficulty goes up. Sitting upright lets the diaphragm work and is frequently the single most effective thing you do for them, so unless their condition prevents it, sit them up.

A patient with reduced consciousness who is breathing adequately gets positioned so their airway is protected — in most systems, on their side. The job is to ensure that if they vomit, it comes out rather than going in.

A patient in shock is where you follow your protocol rather than a remembered rule, because guidance on positioning in shock has changed and varies between systems. Look it up in your own protocol and know what yours says.

Then securing, and the rule that catches people: secure the patient to the device, then secure the device to the vehicle. Both. Every time. A patient perfectly strapped to a stretcher that is not locked into its mount is not secured at all, and an unlocked stretcher in a collision is an enormous heavy object with a person attached to it.

Straps need to be snug. Snug enough that the patient does not move in a sudden stop — and that is the test, not whether they look tidy. Check them again after you have moved, because straps loosen as a patient settles and as the device is handled.

Secure the legs as well as the chest. This gets forgotten, and it matters because patients slide downwards whenever the device tilts — going down stairs, on a ramp, on any incline. Chest straps alone do not prevent that, and a patient sliding down a tilted stretcher is both frightening and dangerous.

Protect against cold at every stage. Patients cool while being moved, and the moving is exactly when they are least covered and most exposed — outdoors, with clothing cut away, with doors open. Cold worsens bleeding, worsens outcomes, and is deeply unpleasant. Cover them, and cover them again after each stage of the move.

And manage the equipment attached to them. Tubing, lines, monitor cables, oxygen tubing and bags all need to be where they will not be caught on a door frame, trapped under the device, or pulled as the stretcher moves. The moment where an oxygen line catches on a door handle is both undignified and genuinely dangerous, and it is completely preventable by thinking about it for five seconds before you start.
read.standard: Packaging comprises preparation of the patient for movement to prevent displacement, entrapment and omission. Positioning constitutes a clinical determination based on patient condition rather than a default. Respiratory compromise indicates upright positioning to permit diaphragmatic excursion, frequently constituting the most effective single intervention, unless otherwise contraindicated. Reduced consciousness with adequate spontaneous ventilation indicates positioning for airway protection, typically lateral, to permit drainage of emesis. Positioning in shock should follow local protocol, as guidance has been revised and varies between systems. Securing requires both fixation of the patient to the device and fixation of the device to the vehicle; a patient secured to an unlocked stretcher is unsecured, and an unrestrained stretcher constitutes a substantial mass hazard in collision. Strap tension must prevent patient movement during sudden deceleration, this functional criterion superseding appearance, and requires re-verification following movement as tension reduces with patient settling and device handling. Lower limb securing is required in addition to thoracic securing, as patients migrate distally whenever the device inclines, including stairways and ramps, which thoracic restraint alone does not prevent. Thermal protection is required at each stage, as patient cooling coincides with periods of maximal exposure through outdoor movement, clothing removal and open doors; hypothermia exacerbates haemorrhage and adverse outcome. Attached equipment including tubing, lines, monitoring cables and oxygen supply requires positioning to prevent snagging, entrapment beneath the device and traction during movement.

concepts.title: Scene hazards, stabilisation and gaining access
key_points: Nobody approaches a crashed vehicle until it has been stabilised and the hazards identified
A vehicle on its wheels can still roll, and a vehicle on its side or roof is inherently unstable
Stabilisation means the vehicle cannot move while people are working in and around it
Traffic is the first hazard at nearly every vehicle incident and it does not stop for you
Fuel, fire and electrical hazards require the engine off and, where trained personnel are present, the battery isolated
Undeployed airbags can fire late — stay out of their path and do not work in front of an undeployed bag
Electric and hybrid vehicles carry high-voltage systems and need specific procedures and trained personnel
Downed power lines make the whole area a no-go until the utility confirms the line is dead
Simple access means getting to the patient without tools — try the doors, try the windows, try asking
Complex access requires tools and training, and it belongs to rescue personnel rather than to you
misconceptions: Approaching before the vehicle is stabilised
Working in front of an undeployed airbag
Assuming a downed line is dead because it is not sparking
Attempting complex access without training or equipment

read.plain:
Nobody approaches a crashed vehicle until it has been stabilised and the hazards identified. That sentence does the most work in this concept, because the instinct on arrival is to walk straight to the person you can see, and that instinct is what gets responders hurt.

Start with stability, because vehicles move more than people expect. A car sitting apparently normally on its wheels can still roll, rock, or settle — particularly with people climbing in and out of it and with the suspension still loaded. A vehicle on its side or on its roof is inherently unstable and will move if anybody leans on it. Stabilisation means making the vehicle unable to move while people work in and around it, using cribbing, chocks, struts and whatever your rescue crews carry. It happens before, not during.

Traffic is the first hazard at nearly every vehicle incident, and it is covered in the roadway safety concept, but the point bears repeating here: the crash is stationary and the traffic is not. It does not stop for you, and the drivers are looking at the wreck rather than at you.

Fuel and fire. Spilled fuel is both a fire hazard and a slip hazard. The engine gets switched off. Where trained personnel are present, the battery is isolated, which removes the ignition source and disables electrical systems. Follow your service's procedure rather than improvising with a battery terminal.

Airbags deserve real attention because they are a hazard people forget. An airbag that has already deployed is spent and harmless apart from residue. An undeployed airbag is a stored explosive charge that can fire late, including after the vehicle's power has been disconnected, because many systems hold a reserve. So do not work in front of an undeployed bag, do not put your body or your head in its path, and be aware that they are not only in the steering wheel — there are side bags, curtain bags and knee bags in modern vehicles.

Electric and hybrid vehicles carry high-voltage systems with cabling that is dangerous to cut and batteries that can reignite hours later. They require specific procedures and trained personnel. Identify the vehicle type early and say so, because it changes the rescue plan.

Downed power lines make the whole area a no-go until the utility confirms the line is dead. A line does not have to spark, move or make noise to be live, and the ground around a downed line can be energised. Nobody approaches, nobody touches the vehicle, and patients inside are told to stay inside — they are safer in the vehicle than stepping out of it.

Then access, which splits in two.

Simple access means reaching the patient without tools. And it starts with the things people skip in the excitement: try the doors, all of them, including the ones that look damaged. Try the windows. Try the tailgate. Ask the patient to unlock it. A surprising number of vehicles that look like they need cutting open have a door that opens perfectly well on the far side.

Complex access requires tools, and it requires training. Cutting, spreading, glass management, roof removal — that work belongs to rescue personnel with the equipment and the training for it. Your job while it happens is the patient, which is the next concept.
read.standard: Approach to a crashed vehicle is prohibited prior to stabilisation and hazard identification. Vehicles retain capacity for movement notwithstanding apparently normal orientation, with rolling, rocking and settling occurring under loaded suspension and occupant movement; vehicles resting on side or roof are inherently unstable. Stabilisation renders the vehicle immobile during operations using cribbing, chocks and struts, and precedes rather than accompanies access. Traffic constitutes the primary hazard at most vehicle incidents. Fuel spillage presents fire and slip hazards; the engine is shut down and, where trained personnel are available, the battery isolated per service procedure to remove ignition sources and disable electrical systems. Deployed airbags are expended and present only residue hazard; undeployed airbags constitute stored explosive charges capable of late deployment including following power disconnection owing to reserve capacitance, and personnel must avoid positioning within their deployment path, noting the presence of steering, side, curtain and knee units in contemporary vehicles. Electric and hybrid vehicles carry high-voltage systems with hazardous cabling and batteries subject to delayed reignition, requiring specific procedures, trained personnel and early identification. Downed conductors render the surrounding area inaccessible pending utility confirmation of de-energisation; conductors may be live without visible or audible indication and surrounding ground may be energised, and vehicle occupants are safer remaining within the vehicle. Simple access comprises patient contact without tools and begins with systematic attempts at all doors including damaged ones, windows, tailgate and patient-operated unlocking. Complex access requires tools and training and is the responsibility of rescue personnel.

concepts.title: Extrication roles and protecting the patient
key_points: Extrication is a team activity with defined roles, and everybody works to one plan
One person is in command of the incident and one person is responsible for the patient
Your job during extrication is the patient, not the tools — stay with them and keep working
Tell the rescue team what the patient's condition needs, because it changes how fast and how they cut
Rescue needs to know if the patient is deteriorating, because that changes the plan from tidy to quick

read.plain:
Extrication is a team activity with defined roles, and its success depends on everybody working to one plan rather than several good intentions happening simultaneously.

So there is one person in command of the incident, and one person responsible for the patient. Know which you are. On most EMS calls at a rescue, you are the second.

Which leads to the most useful instruction in this concept: your job is the patient, not the tools. The pull towards the interesting equipment is real, and it is wrong. Somebody has to be inside or alongside that vehicle managing the airway, controlling bleeding, monitoring, reassuring and reassessing, and that is you. Get in, stay in, and keep working.

Then the communication that makes the whole thing work. Tell the rescue team what the patient's condition needs, because it changes how they do their job. A stable patient in a complicated vehicle allows a methodical, tidy extrication that takes twenty minutes and does minimal further harm. A patient who is deteriorating changes the plan entirely — the team will accept a rougher, faster route out because time has become the dominant factor. They cannot make that judgement from outside the car. You have to tell them, and you have to tell them when it changes.

That is worth emphasising. Rescue crews will frequently ask for an update, but do not wait to be asked. If the patient's condition worsens, say so immediately and clearly, because the plan needs to change and the people who would change it are outside holding equipment.

Protect the patient physically throughout. Glass, dust and debris from cutting and glass management — cover them, including the face and eyes. Noise, which is genuinely extreme; hearing protection where it is available. Cold, because a patient sitting in a wrecked vehicle with the roof and doors removed is exposed to the weather for a long period. And the general assault of the whole environment.

Explain what is about to happen before it happens. Extrication is terrifying from the inside — enormous noise, the car shaking, glass breaking, metal tearing, and strangers in masks working around you. A patient who has been told that the next noise will be the roof being cut and that it will be very loud copes with it very differently from one who has not. Keep talking throughout, and say when the next loud thing is coming.

Maintain manual spinal stabilisation as your protocol directs while the vehicle is being worked on, because the vehicle moves as it is cut and spread.

Reassess frequently. This is where long extrications fail: everyone is busy, the noise makes conversation difficult, the patient is partly hidden, and twenty minutes pass in which nobody has actually rechecked anything. Set yourself a rhythm and keep it.

And the patient comes out along the path of least harm — in the direction their injuries allow, through the opening that requires the least movement of them, rather than through whichever hole was easiest to make.
read.standard: Extrication constitutes a coordinated team operation with defined roles executed under a single plan. Command of the incident and responsibility for the patient are separately designated; EMS personnel at rescue incidents typically hold the latter. The patient care role requires continuous patient attendance rather than participation in tool operations, comprising airway management, haemorrhage control, monitoring, reassurance and reassessment. Communication of patient condition to the rescue team is essential, as condition determines extrication method and pace: stable patients permit methodical extrication minimising secondary injury, whereas deterioration justifies accelerated extrication accepting increased movement. Rescue personnel cannot assess condition from outside the vehicle, and deterioration must be communicated immediately and unprompted. Physical protection comprises covering against glass, dust and debris including the face and eyes, hearing protection against extreme noise where available, and thermal protection during prolonged exposure following roof and door removal. Anticipatory explanation is required, as extrication produces extreme noise, vehicle movement, glass breakage and metal deformation; forewarning materially affects patient tolerance, and continuous communication should be maintained. Manual spinal stabilisation is maintained per protocol during vehicle manipulation, as the vehicle moves during cutting and spreading. Frequent reassessment is required, as prolonged extrication with environmental noise and restricted patient access predisposes to unrecognised deterioration. Patient removal follows the path producing least harm, determined by injury pattern and required movement rather than ease of access creation.

eli_new.analogy: A stable patient buys the rescue team twenty tidy minutes. A deteriorating one buys them nothing, and only you can tell them which situation they are in.
eli_new.body: Your job is the patient, not the tools. The pull towards the interesting equipment is real and it is wrong — get in the car and stay there.

concepts.title: The incident command system
key_points: The incident command system is a standard structure for organising any incident, large or small
Its purpose is one plan, clear roles and a manageable span of control
There is always exactly one person in command, and command is formally transferred rather than drifting
Span of control means one supervisor oversees a manageable number of people, commonly cited as around three to seven
Common terminology matters — plain language rather than agency-specific codes, so everyone understands
The system scales: a small incident may be one person, a large one has sections and branches
Unified command lets several agencies command together when an incident crosses their responsibilities
You report to one supervisor and you receive assignments from that person only
Report in, take your assignment, work within it, and report back — freelancing is the danger
Accountability means command knows who is on scene and where they are, which matters when things go wrong
misconceptions: Freelancing rather than working within an assignment
Taking direction from several people at once
Using agency-specific radio codes at a multi-agency incident
Leaving command ambiguous or unannounced

read.plain:
The incident command system is a standard structure for organising an incident — any incident, from a two-vehicle collision to a disaster. It is worth learning properly because it is used by every agency you will work alongside, and because most of it is common sense with names attached.

Its purpose is three things: one plan, clear roles, and a span of control that a human being can actually manage.

Start with command. There is always exactly one person in command of an incident. Not a committee, not whoever happens to be most senior, and not everybody a bit. One person, identified, and known to everyone on scene. When command changes — because someone more appropriate arrives, or the first person hands over — it is transferred formally and announced, with a proper briefing. Command that drifts quietly from one person to another is command that nobody actually holds.

Span of control is the idea that one supervisor can only effectively oversee a limited number of people. The commonly cited range is around three to seven, with five often given as the working number. When more people or more tasks arrive than that, the structure grows: you add another level, so each supervisor stays within a manageable span. That is the whole reason large incidents develop layers — not bureaucracy, but arithmetic about attention.

Common terminology is a genuinely important and frequently overlooked principle. Everyone uses plain language rather than agency-specific radio codes. A code that means one thing to your service may mean something different or nothing at all to the fire crew and the police on the same channel, and on a bad day that ambiguity costs time or lives. Say what you mean in words.

The system scales in both directions. A small incident might be one person doing everything, which is still incident command. A large one develops sections and branches with defined responsibilities. The structure grows to fit the incident rather than the incident being forced into a structure.

Unified command exists for incidents that cross agency responsibilities — a vehicle fire with casualties on a highway involves fire, EMS, police and the highway authority, and no single agency owns the whole thing. Unified command lets them command together, with one shared plan rather than several parallel ones.

Now the part that applies to you personally, every time.

You report to one supervisor, and you take assignments from that person only. If someone else gives you a task, you take it back to your supervisor. This feels rigid and it exists for a reason: taking direction from three people means being in three places, none of them where you were needed.

Report in, take your assignment, work within it, and report back when it is done or when you cannot do it. The failure mode with a name is freelancing — seeing something that needs doing and going off to do it without telling anyone. It is almost always well intentioned, and it is dangerous: command believes you are somewhere you are not, the task you left is not done, and if the scene goes bad nobody knows where to look for you.

Which brings in accountability. Command needs to know who is on scene and where they are. That is not administration — it is the mechanism by which people get found when a building changes or a scene turns.
read.standard: The incident command system provides a standardised organisational structure applicable to incidents of any scale, employed across responding agencies. Its objectives comprise unified planning, defined role allocation and maintenance of manageable span of control. Command resides with exactly one designated individual known to all personnel; command transfer occurs formally with announcement and briefing, undocumented drift of command being a recognised failure. Span of control denotes the number of personnel one supervisor may effectively oversee, commonly cited as three to seven with five as a working figure; exceedance triggers structural expansion by addition of supervisory levels. Common terminology requires plain language in preference to agency-specific codes, as code meanings differ between agencies operating on shared channels. The structure scales bidirectionally, from single-provider incidents to incidents requiring sections and branches, expanding to fit the incident. Unified command applies where incidents cross agency responsibilities, permitting joint command under a single shared plan. Individual providers report to a single supervisor and accept assignments only from that individual, referring tasks received from others back through their supervisor. The operational sequence comprises reporting in, accepting assignment, working within it, and reporting completion or inability. Freelancing, denoting self-directed activity outside assignment without notification, constitutes the principal individual failure mode, producing inaccurate command awareness of personnel location, incomplete assigned tasks, and inability to locate personnel during scene deterioration. Accountability systems maintain command awareness of personnel presence and location.

eli_new.analogy: Span of control is arithmetic about attention, not bureaucracy. One person can watch about five things properly, so when there are twenty things you add a layer.
eli_new.body: Freelancing is the dangerous one, and it is always well intentioned. Command thinks you are somewhere you are not, your actual task is not done, and if the scene turns nobody knows where to look.

concepts.title: Multiple casualty incidents
key_points: A multiple casualty incident is one where the patients exceed the resources immediately available
That definition is relative — three patients can be an MCI for one ambulance in a rural system
The first unit's job is size-up, declaring, requesting and establishing command, not patient care
Resisting the pull to treat the first patient you see is the hardest and most important discipline
Request resources early and generously, because you can always cancel what you do not need
Give a clear initial report: location, what happened, approximate numbers, hazards and access
Functional roles get assigned as people arrive: triage, treatment, transport and staging
Staging keeps arriving units in one known place so they can be assigned rather than converging
Transport tracks where each patient goes, because that record is needed afterwards and nobody reconstructs it later
The aim shifts from doing everything possible for one patient to doing the most good for the most patients
misconceptions: Treating the first patient instead of sizing up and declaring
Under-requesting resources on the first report
Letting arriving units self-deploy rather than staging
Failing to record where patients were transported

read.plain:
A multiple casualty incident is one where the number of patients exceeds the resources immediately available. That is the definition, and the important word in it is relative. An MCI is not defined by a number of patients; it is defined by the relationship between patients and resources. Three patients is an ordinary day for a busy urban system and a full-blown MCI for a single ambulance an hour from anywhere. Judge it against what you have.

The first unit on scene has a specific job, and it is not patient care. It is size-up, declare, request, and establish command.

This is the hardest discipline in EMS operations, so it is worth being blunt about it. You will arrive and there will be an injured person in front of you, visible and audible and clearly needing help. Every instinct you have will say to start treating them. And if you do, you have removed the only person who could have organised the incident, and the twelve other patients you have not yet found will wait considerably longer for everything. The first crew treats nobody. They organise. It feels wrong and it is right.

Give a clear initial report. Location, what has happened, approximate number of patients, hazards, access and where you want incoming units to come in from. Approximate is fine — an early rough number is far more useful than an accurate one in ten minutes.

Request early and generously. It is easy to cancel resources that turn out not to be needed and very hard to catch up when you under-called at the start. The cost of over-requesting is some inconvenience; the cost of under-requesting is measured in patient outcomes.

Then roles get assigned as people arrive, organised by function rather than by rank.

Triage sorts the patients and works out who needs what first. Treatment provides care in the treatment area, grouped by priority. Transport decides who goes where and in what order, matching patients to available vehicles and to hospital capability. Staging holds arriving units in one known location so they can be assigned deliberately.

Staging deserves a note because it is what stops the second failure mode of MCIs. Without staging, every arriving unit drives to where the patients are, parks wherever there is space, and disappears into the incident. Within ten minutes there are vehicles blocking each other, crews working unsupervised, and nobody knows what resources are actually available. Staging keeps them findable and assignable.

Transport tracking matters more than people expect on the day. Somebody records which patient went in which vehicle to which hospital. Afterwards — sometimes hours afterwards, sometimes for days — families, hospitals and investigators need that information, and it cannot be reconstructed from memory. Write it down at the time or it is gone.

And underneath all of it is a shift in aim that takes getting used to. Normally you do everything possible for the patient in front of you. In an MCI, you do the most good for the most patients, which sometimes means moving past someone you could have helped in order to reach several people who need you more. That is not callousness; it is the arithmetic of a situation where the resources are finite, and it is why triage exists.
read.standard: A multiple casualty incident denotes an event where patient numbers exceed immediately available resources; the definition is relative to available capability rather than absolute patient count, such that small numbers may constitute an MCI in resource-limited settings. The initial arriving unit performs size-up, declaration, resource request and command establishment rather than patient care; commencement of individual patient treatment removes the only available organising capacity and delays care to undiscovered patients. The initial report comprises location, incident nature, approximate patient numbers, hazards, access and ingress routing, with early approximation preferred to delayed accuracy. Resource requests should be early and generous, as cancellation is operationally trivial relative to the consequences of initial under-request. Functional role assignment occurs as personnel arrive: triage sorts patients by priority; treatment delivers care within priority-grouped areas; transport allocates patients to vehicles and destinations by capability; staging holds arriving units at a designated location for deliberate assignment. Absence of staging produces uncontrolled self-deployment with vehicle congestion, unsupervised working and loss of resource visibility. Transport tracking records patient, vehicle and destination contemporaneously, as this information is required subsequently by families, facilities and investigators and cannot be reconstructed retrospectively. The operational objective shifts from maximal intervention for the individual patient to maximal benefit across the patient population, which may require deferring treatable patients to reach those of greater priority.

eli_new.analogy: The first crew treats nobody. It feels wrong, and it is right — because the person who starts treating is the person who was going to organise the whole incident.
eli_new.body: An MCI is not a number of patients. It is patients exceeding what you have, which means three can be an MCI for one ambulance an hour from anywhere.
