concepts.title: START triage
key_points: Triage sorts patients by priority so that limited resources do the most good
START stands for Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment, and it is designed to be fast rather than accurate
Aim for a very short assessment per patient — seconds, not minutes
Only three interventions are performed during triage: open the airway, control major bleeding, and move on
Step one: anyone who can walk is directed to a designated area and tagged minor
Step two, breathing: if not breathing, open the airway; breathing now means immediate, still not breathing means deceased
Step three, breathing rate: above 30 is immediate, otherwise continue
Step four, perfusion: absent radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds is immediate, otherwise continue

read.plain:
Triage sorts patients by priority so that limited resources do the most good. It is the mechanism by which an overwhelmed scene becomes a manageable one.

START stands for Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment, and the design goal is worth understanding: it is built to be fast, not to be accurate. A system that sorted perfectly but took three minutes a patient would be useless on a scene with forty patients. START accepts that it will occasionally get an individual wrong in order to sort everybody quickly, and that trade is deliberate.

So the pace is seconds per patient. Not minutes. If you find yourself spending a minute on someone, you have stopped triaging and started treating.

Which leads to the rule that people find hardest: during triage you perform only three interventions. Open the airway. Control major bleeding. Move on. That is the entire list. Everything else — splinting, dressing, reassurance, a full assessment — happens later in the treatment area, by people whose job that is. If you stop to treat during triage, patients you have not reached yet are waiting, and some of them are worse than the one in front of you.

The five steps.

Step one. Anyone who can walk is directed to a designated area and tagged minor. This one step frequently removes the majority of patients from the problem in about fifteen seconds, and it is the highest-value thing in the whole system. Say it loudly and clearly: everyone who can hear me and can walk, go to that point over there.

Step two, breathing. Is the patient breathing? If not, open the airway with a simple manoeuvre. If they start breathing, they are immediate. If they still do not breathe, they are tagged deceased and you move on. That is the hardest instruction in EMS and it is correct in this context: resources spent on one non-breathing patient are resources taken from several who can be saved.

Step three, rate. If they are breathing faster than about thirty breaths a minute, they are immediate. If not, carry on.

Step four, perfusion. Check a radial pulse, or capillary refill. No radial pulse, or refill longer than about two seconds, means immediate. Otherwise carry on. Control any major bleeding you find at this point — that is the second of your three permitted interventions.

Step five, mental status. Can they follow a simple command — squeeze my hand, open your eyes? If not, immediate. If they can, they are delayed.

So the categories come out as: minor for the walking wounded, delayed for those who pass every step, immediate for anyone who fails breathing, rate, perfusion or mental status, and deceased for those who do not breathe after the airway is opened.

And the last principle matters as much as the algorithm: triage is repeated. A tag is a snapshot of one moment, not a verdict. Patients deteriorate, and someone tagged delayed twenty minutes ago may be immediate now. Retriage is built into the process, and the treatment area exists partly so that somebody is watching for exactly that.
read.standard: Triage prioritises patients to maximise benefit from limited resources. START, denoting Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment, prioritises speed over accuracy by design, accepting individual misclassification to achieve rapid population sorting; assessment duration should be measured in seconds. Permitted interventions during triage are limited to three: airway opening, major haemorrhage control, and progression to the next patient; all other care is deferred to the treatment area, as treatment during triage delays assessment of unreached and potentially higher-priority patients. The algorithm proceeds in five steps. Ambulatory patients are directed to a designated area and categorised minor, frequently removing the majority of patients rapidly. Respiratory assessment follows: apnoea prompts airway opening, with resumption of respiration categorised immediate and persistent apnoea categorised deceased. Respiratory rate above approximately 30 per minute is categorised immediate. Perfusion assessment by radial pulse or capillary refill categorises absent radial pulse or refill exceeding approximately 2 seconds as immediate, with major haemorrhage controlled at this point. Mental status assessment categorises inability to follow simple commands as immediate and ability as delayed. Resulting categories comprise minor for ambulatory patients, delayed for those passing all criteria, immediate for failure at any criterion, and deceased for persistent apnoea following airway opening. Triage is repeated, as categorisation represents a single time point and patients deteriorate; the treatment area provides the observation supporting retriage.

eli_new.analogy: START is built to be fast rather than right. It accepts getting the occasional individual wrong in order to sort everybody quickly, and that trade is the whole design.
eli_new.body: Three interventions only: open the airway, stop major bleeding, move on. If you are doing anything else, you have stopped triaging.

concepts.title: JumpSTART and triaging children
key_points: JumpSTART is the paediatric counterpart to START, because children are not small adults physiologically
The core difference is that children arrest from respiratory causes, so an apnoeic child gets a ventilation attempt
Infants who cannot walk are assessed rather than automatically tagged minor
Able to walk means minor, as in the adult system
If not breathing, open the airway; if breathing starts, immediate
If still not breathing, check for a pulse: no pulse means deceased
If there is a pulse but no breathing, give five rescue breaths — this is the JumpSTART difference
Breathing after those breaths means immediate; still apnoeic means deceased
Respiratory rate below 15 or above 45 is immediate, otherwise check perfusion and then mental status

misconceptions: Applying adult START unmodified to children

read.plain:
JumpSTART is the paediatric counterpart to START, and it exists because children are not small adults physiologically. Applying the adult algorithm unmodified to a child produces the wrong answer in a predictable way.

The reason is the one that runs through all of paediatrics: children arrest from respiratory causes. An adult found apnoeic on a disaster scene has usually had a catastrophic event and is genuinely unsalvageable within triage constraints. A child found apnoeic may have a perfectly good heart that simply needs some air, and a very short intervention may restart them. So JumpSTART builds that intervention into the algorithm, where START does not.

JumpSTART is intended for children, with the commonly taught range being roughly one to eight years — and in practice, if a patient looks like a child, use it; if they look like an adult, use START. Do not spend triage time deciding.

The sequence.

Can they walk? If yes, minor, same as the adult system. There is one modification: infants who are too young to walk are not automatically tagged minor for that reason. They are carried to the minor area and assessed there, because the whole logic of the walking step — that walking demonstrates adequate airway, breathing, circulation and mental status — does not apply to someone who has never walked.

Breathing? If yes, go to rate. If no, open the airway. If they start breathing, immediate.

If they still are not breathing, check for a pulse. No pulse, deceased.

And here is the JumpSTART difference, the one thing to remember above all: if there is a pulse but no breathing, give five rescue breaths. That is the modification, it is the reason the system exists, and it is what people forget.

If breathing starts after those breaths, immediate. If they remain apnoeic, deceased. So in JumpSTART, an apnoeic child with a pulse gets one short intervention before being tagged, and no other patient in either system does.

For breathing children, the rate thresholds differ from the adult. Below 15 or above 45 is immediate. Both ends matter — a child breathing too slowly is as concerning as one breathing too fast, and a slow rate in a child is an ominous sign rather than a calm one.

If the rate falls between those, check perfusion. A palpable peripheral pulse is required; absent means immediate.

Then mental status, which uses AVPU rather than the adult follow-commands test, because many children are too young to follow commands reliably even when perfectly well. Alert, responds to Voice, or responds to Pain appropriately — meaning localising, withdrawing, pushing you away — is delayed. Inappropriate responses such as posturing, or unresponsive, is immediate.

That AVPU substitution is worth understanding rather than memorising, because it is the same principle as the walking step: you cannot use a test the patient could not pass when well.
read.standard: JumpSTART constitutes the paediatric adaptation of START, developed because paediatric physiology differs materially from adult. The principal distinction derives from the predominance of respiratory aetiology in paediatric arrest: apnoeic adults in disaster triage are generally unsalvageable within triage constraints, whereas apnoeic children may retain adequate cardiac function and respond to brief ventilatory intervention, which JumpSTART incorporates. Application is indicated for paediatric patients, commonly cited as approximately one to eight years, with practical determination by apparent developmental stage rather than triage-time deliberation. The algorithm proceeds as follows. Ambulatory patients are categorised minor. Pre-ambulatory infants are not automatically categorised minor, as the walking criterion presupposes demonstrated ambulatory capability; they are carried to the minor area and assessed. Apnoeic patients undergo airway opening, with resumption of respiration categorised immediate. Persistent apnoea prompts pulse assessment: absent pulse is categorised deceased; present pulse prompts administration of five rescue breaths, constituting the defining JumpSTART modification. Resumption of respiration thereafter is categorised immediate; persistent apnoea is categorised deceased. In breathing patients, respiratory rate below 15 or above 45 per minute is categorised immediate, bradypnoea carrying equivalent significance to tachypnoea. Intermediate rates prompt perfusion assessment by palpable peripheral pulse, absence categorising immediate. Mental status employs AVPU rather than command-following, as young children may not reliably follow commands when well: alert, voice-responsive, or appropriately pain-responsive with localisation or withdrawal is categorised delayed; inappropriate responses including posturing, or unresponsiveness, is categorised immediate.

eli_new.analogy: A child found apnoeic may have a perfectly good heart that needs some air. That single fact is why JumpSTART exists and why it has five breaths in it.
eli_new.body: The one thing to remember: pulse but no breathing means five rescue breaths. Nothing else in either triage system gets an intervention like that, and it is exactly what people forget.

concepts.title: Recognising a hazmat incident and using the guidebook
key_points: The most dangerous hazmat incident is the one nobody recognised as one
Recognise from a distance, upwind and uphill, using binoculars rather than proximity
Clues: the occupancy, the container shape, placards and labels, spilled material, vapour clouds, odours and dead vegetation or animals
Several people with similar symptoms in the same place is a hazmat presentation until proved otherwise
Transport placards carry a hazard class number and often a four-digit UN identification number
Fixed facilities often use a diamond with health, flammability and reactivity ratings and a special-hazard section
Shipping papers identify the load and are carried in known places on each mode of transport
The Emergency Response Guidebook turns an identification into an action plan and initial distances
Yellow finds by number, blue finds by name, orange gives the actions and green gives the distances

misconceptions: Approaching to read a placard
Assuming an absent odour means an absent hazard
Treating multiple similar patients as a coincidence
Trying to identify a material at close range

read.plain:
The most dangerous hazardous materials incident is the one nobody recognised as one. Crews walk in, treat patients, and become patients. So recognition is the whole skill, and it happens from a distance.

Approach upwind and uphill. Stop well back. Use binoculars — they are on the vehicle for exactly this, and the reason they exist is that reading a placard should never require being close enough for the placard to matter.

The clues.

The occupancy: what is this place? Industrial sites, agricultural premises, laboratories, plating shops, pool supply stores, farms with chemical stores. What happens here tells you what might be released here.

The container shape: tankers and cylinders and drums have shapes that indicate what they hold, and a shape that does not belong — a pressurised cylinder where there should not be one — is information.

Placards and labels: the diamond-shaped signs on vehicles and containers.

The physical evidence: spilled liquid, a vapour cloud, unusual odours, fog where there should be none, bubbling or boiling, discoloured surfaces, and dead or distressed vegetation, insects or animals. Dead birds around a scene is a warning that costs nothing to notice.

And the clue that gets missed most often, because it presents as medicine rather than as a hazard: several people with similar symptoms in the same place. Multiple patients with the same complaint, in the same building, at the same time, is a hazardous materials or exposure presentation until proved otherwise. It is not a coincidence, it is not food poisoning until you have excluded the alternative, and walking in to treat them is exactly how responders are injured.

Be careful about odours in both directions. An odour tells you something is there. The absence of an odour tells you very little, because many dangerous materials have no smell at all, and some destroy your sense of smell as part of the exposure. And if you can smell it, you are already in it.

On identification. Transport placards carry a hazard class number indicating the type of danger, and frequently a four-digit UN identification number that specifies the material. Fixed facilities often display a diamond divided into sections — health, flammability and reactivity, each rated on a scale, plus a section for special hazards such as water reactivity. Shipping papers describe the load and live in known places: with the driver in a road vehicle, with the conductor on a train, on the bridge of a vessel.

Then the Emergency Response Guidebook, which turns an identification into an action plan. Its structure is colour-coded and worth knowing cold, because in an incident you want to open it once and land in the right place.

The white pages at the front and back tell you how to use it and what to do first. The yellow section finds the material by its four-digit UN number. The blue section finds it by name. Both send you to the same orange section, which holds the guide pages: fire, spill, first aid, protective clothing, and what to do in the first minutes. And the green section gives initial isolation and protective action distances for the materials that need them.

So: yellow by number, blue by name, orange for what to do, green for how far back.

And hold on to what your job actually is at an EMT level. Recognise, retreat, isolate, notify. Recognise that this is a hazmat incident, get back and stay back, keep everyone else out, and call the people whose job this is. Identification from a safe distance is useful. Identification from close range is how you become the second call.
read.standard: Unrecognised hazardous materials incidents pose the greatest danger, as responders enter contaminated environments and become casualties. Recognition is performed at distance from an upwind and uphill position using binoculars, as placard legibility should not require hazardous proximity. Recognition indicators comprise occupancy type including industrial, agricultural, laboratory and chemical retail premises; container configuration, with pressurised, tank and drum geometries indicating contents and anomalous containers constituting information; placards and labels; and physical evidence including spilled liquid, vapour clouds, unusual odours, unexplained fog, bubbling, surface discolouration and dead or distressed vegetation, insects or animals. Multiple patients presenting with similar symptoms at a common location constitutes a hazardous materials or exposure presentation pending exclusion and is the most frequently missed indicator. Olfactory evidence is asymmetrically informative: odour presence indicates release, whereas absence excludes little, as many hazardous materials are odourless and some produce olfactory fatigue; perceptible odour indicates existing exposure. Transport placards display a hazard class number and frequently a four-digit UN identification number. Fixed facilities commonly display a sectioned diamond rating health, flammability and reactivity with a special hazards section. Shipping papers are located with the driver in road transport, the conductor in rail transport, and on the bridge in marine transport. The Emergency Response Guidebook is organised by colour: white sections describe use and initial actions; yellow indexes by UN number; blue indexes by name; orange contains guide pages covering fire, spill, first aid and protective clothing; green provides initial isolation and protective action distances. The EMT role comprises recognition, withdrawal, isolation and notification rather than close-range identification.

eli_new.analogy: Binoculars exist so that reading a placard never requires being close enough for the placard to matter.
eli_new.body: Several people with the same symptoms in the same building at the same time is a hazmat presentation until proved otherwise. It presents as medicine, which is exactly why it gets missed.

story.title: All four of them
story.dispatch: Medic 6 — four people unwell in a commercial basement.
story.body:
Four patients, one room, the same symptoms, and the call had come in as illness.

Somebody stopped at the top of the stairs and said the word out loud before anyone went down.

They went back up, called it in, and none of them became the fifth.

concepts.title: Zones and scene control
key_points: Hazmat scenes are divided into three zones, and the division is what keeps contamination from spreading
The hot zone contains the hazard, and only trained personnel in appropriate protection enter it
No patient care happens in the hot zone beyond removing the patient from it
The warm zone is the decontamination corridor, where contamination is reduced on the way out
The cold zone is everything beyond: command, staging, treatment and transport, and nothing contaminated enters it
Movement runs one way — from hot, through warm, into cold — and never back the other way
EMT-level providers work in the cold zone unless specifically trained and equipped otherwise
Zone boundaries are set by the hazard, the wind and the terrain, and they can change if the wind changes
Control entry and exit deliberately, because uncontrolled movement is how a contained incident spreads
Contaminated patients do not enter the ambulance, and contaminated responders do not enter the cold zone
misconceptions: Entering the hot zone without training or protection
Allowing a contaminated patient into the ambulance
Treating zone boundaries as fixed regardless of wind
Letting people move back from cold into warm casually
exam_favorites: EMTs work in the cold zone

read.plain:
Hazmat scenes are divided into three zones, and that division is the mechanism that stops a contained incident from becoming a spreading one. It is worth understanding as a system rather than as three definitions.

The hot zone is the area containing the hazard, and it extends far enough out that everything inside it is potentially contaminated. Only personnel who are trained and wearing appropriate protective equipment enter it. And the rule about care is absolute: no patient care happens in the hot zone beyond removing the patient from it. There is no assessment, no treatment, no vital signs. Entry teams get patients out; care begins once they are out.

The warm zone is the decontamination corridor — the controlled path between hot and cold, where contamination is reduced. This is where decontamination happens, where protective equipment comes off in a defined sequence, and where trained personnel with appropriate protection work. Life-saving interventions may be performed here by appropriately trained and protected people, but it is not where general patient care happens.

The cold zone is everything beyond, and it is the clean side: command post, staging, the treatment area, the transport area, and the ambulances. Nothing contaminated enters it. That is the entire definition.

The principle that ties the three together is one-way movement. Hot, through warm, into cold. Never the other direction without going through the whole process again. People and equipment and patients flow one way, and every time somebody shortcuts that — walks back in for a piece of kit, steps out of the corridor early, hands something across a boundary — the incident gets bigger.

Where do you work? Unless you are specifically trained and equipped for it, you work in the cold zone. That is not a limitation to be apologetic about; it is the correct place for an EMT to be. Your patients arrive to you decontaminated, and you provide the care you would provide to anyone, in the place where it is safe to do so.

Zone boundaries are set by the hazard, the wind and the terrain, and the important operational consequence is that they are not fixed. If the wind shifts, the zones move. A cold zone that was safe twenty minutes ago may not be safe now, and the treatment area, the staging area and the command post may all need to move. Somebody must be watching the wind, and everybody must be prepared to relocate.

Control the entry and exit points deliberately. Uncontrolled movement across boundaries is precisely how a contained incident spreads, and it is usually done by well-meaning people in a hurry.

And two consequences to hold onto, because they are the ones tested and the ones that matter on scene. Contaminated patients do not enter the ambulance — an ambulance interior is impossible to decontaminate properly and a contaminated vehicle is out of service and a hazard in itself. And contaminated responders do not enter the cold zone. Both rules feel obstructive in the moment, and both exist because somebody previously found out what happens otherwise.
read.standard: Hazardous materials incidents are organised into three control zones, the division constituting the mechanism preventing contamination spread. The hot zone encompasses the hazard and surrounding potentially contaminated area; entry is restricted to trained personnel in appropriate protective equipment. Patient care within the hot zone is limited to extraction; assessment, treatment and vital sign measurement do not occur there. The warm zone constitutes the decontamination corridor, providing a controlled route between hot and cold zones where contamination reduction and sequenced protective equipment removal occur, staffed by trained and protected personnel; life-saving intervention by appropriately trained personnel may occur here, but general patient care does not. The cold zone comprises all remaining area including command post, staging, treatment and transport areas and vehicles, into which no contaminated person, patient or equipment enters. Movement proceeds unidirectionally from hot through warm to cold, with reverse movement requiring full reprocessing; boundary shortcuts including equipment retrieval, premature corridor exit and cross-boundary transfer expand the incident. EMT-level providers operate in the cold zone unless specifically trained and equipped otherwise, receiving decontaminated patients. Zone boundaries are determined by hazard characteristics, wind and terrain and are therefore dynamic; wind shift requires zone relocation, potentially including treatment, staging and command areas, requiring continuous wind monitoring and relocation readiness. Entry and exit points require deliberate control, as uncontrolled boundary movement spreads contained incidents. Contaminated patients do not enter ambulances, as vehicle interiors cannot be adequately decontaminated and contaminated vehicles are both unavailable and hazardous; contaminated responders do not enter the cold zone.

eli_new.analogy: Hot, warm, cold, one way only. Every shortcut across a boundary makes the incident bigger, and shortcuts are always taken by well-meaning people in a hurry.
eli_new.body: If the wind shifts, the zones move. A cold zone that was safe twenty minutes ago may not be safe now, and that includes wherever you parked.

concepts.title: Decontamination and contaminated patients
key_points: Decontamination removes or reduces the contaminant before the patient enters the clean side
Removing clothing removes a large proportion of the contamination and is the highest-value first step
Brush or blot dry powders off before adding water, because water can activate some materials
Then wash with copious water, working from the head downwards, protecting the airway and eyes
Bag and isolate clothing and belongings, and record what was removed
Decontamination happens before the patient enters the ambulance, not after
Protect yourself first — a contaminated responder cannot treat anybody
Consult medical direction and the guidebook, and treat symptoms as your protocol directs
Avoid becoming a secondary casualty by contact with the patient, their clothing or their vomit
Runoff water is contaminated too, and it must be contained where the incident allows
misconceptions: Adding water to a dry powder before brushing it off
Loading a contaminated patient to decontaminate en route
Handling contaminated clothing without protection
Forgetting that runoff is contaminated

read.plain:
Decontamination removes or reduces the contaminant before the patient reaches the clean side. It is the process that makes the rest of the care possible.

The highest-value single step is removing the patient's clothing. It is simple, it needs no equipment, and it removes a large proportion of the contamination in one action, because most of what has landed on a person is on their clothes rather than on them. If you take one thing from this concept, it is that undressing the patient is the intervention.

Sequence matters with dry materials. Brush or blot dry powders off before you apply any water. Some materials react with water — including violently — and turning a dry powder into a wet slurry can spread it, drive it into skin, or make it considerably more dangerous. Dry first, then wet.

Then wash with copious amounts of water. Volume is what does the work. Work from the head downwards so you are not washing contaminant over areas already cleaned, and protect the airway and the eyes while you do it — the eyes in particular need irrigation in their own right if they are involved.

Bag and isolate the clothing and personal belongings, keep them secure, and record what was removed and where it went. Patients care about their belongings, and the items themselves may be needed for identification of the substance.

Decontamination happens before the patient enters the ambulance. Not on the way. Not partially, with the rest done later. An ambulance interior cannot be decontaminated to any real standard, which means a contaminated patient in the back produces a contaminated vehicle, a contaminated crew, and a contaminated hospital bay at the other end. That single rule prevents an enormous amount of harm.

Protect yourself first, which is worth restating because the instinct fights it. A contaminated responder cannot treat anybody, and instead becomes a patient who consumes resources. That is not selfishness, it is arithmetic.

For the medicine itself: consult medical direction and the guidebook, and treat symptoms as your protocol directs. The guidebook's orange section carries first aid guidance for the specific material, and medical direction can advise on what the exposure requires. This is one of the clearest cases where the answer is not in your head and is not supposed to be.

Stay alert to secondary contamination through the routes people forget: contact with the patient's skin, their clothing, their hair, their belongings, and their vomit. A patient who has ingested or inhaled something may off-gas or may vomit contaminated material, and the person holding the bowl is exposed.

And remember that runoff water is contaminated. The water that has just washed a patient is now a hazardous material, and where the incident allows, it should be contained rather than allowed to run into drains or watercourses. That is a hazmat team responsibility rather than yours, but knowing it stops you from making it worse.
read.standard: Decontamination reduces or removes contaminant prior to patient entry into the clean zone. Clothing removal constitutes the highest-yield initial intervention, requiring no equipment and eliminating a substantial proportion of contaminant, as the majority of deposited material resides on clothing rather than skin. Dry contaminants require brushing or blotting prior to water application, as certain materials react with water, potentially violently, and hydration may disperse material, drive it into skin or increase hazard. Irrigation employs copious water volume, proceeding cranially to caudally to avoid recontamination of cleaned areas, with airway and ocular protection maintained and separate ocular irrigation where indicated. Clothing and personal effects are bagged, isolated, secured and documented, as items may be required for substance identification. Decontamination precedes ambulance entry without exception, as vehicle interiors cannot be adequately decontaminated and contaminated transport produces contaminated vehicles, personnel and receiving facilities. Provider self-protection precedes patient care, as a contaminated provider becomes a resource-consuming casualty. Clinical management proceeds by consultation with medical direction and the Emergency Response Guidebook orange section first aid guidance, with symptomatic treatment per protocol. Secondary contamination routes include patient skin, clothing, hair, personal effects and emesis, with off-gassing and contaminated vomitus presenting risk to attending personnel. Runoff water constitutes hazardous material requiring containment where operationally feasible, this being a hazardous materials team responsibility.

eli_new.analogy: Undressing the patient is the intervention. It takes no equipment, it takes seconds, and most of what landed on them is on their clothes rather than on them.
eli_new.body: Dry first, then wet. Brushing a powder off is safe; adding water to it can make it react, spread it, or drive it into the skin.

story.title: Dry first
story.dispatch: Rescue 4 — patient covered in a dry chemical powder.
story.body:
Somebody reached for a hose, which is the obvious thing to reach for.

Somebody else said to brush it off first, and they did, with a gloved hand and a soft brush.

The guidebook entry, read afterwards, said the material reacted with water.
